title: Building Construction
intro: Concise Notes for Competitive Exams — Extended Edition (lectures + online material, diagrams, MCQs & links)
Master handbook covering: Building Construction + Exam Practice Pack
Overlapping topics have been merged into one chapter and repeated points removed. Practice MCQs for all parts are near the end; the answer key is the last chapter.

b: Substructure: part below plinth level (foundation). Superstructure: part above plinth.
Main components: foundation, plinth, walls/columns, floors, doors & windows, sills, lintels, stairs, roof, parapet, finishes, services.
Plinth: portion between ground level and ground-floor level; min height ≈ 45 cm above ground.
Load-bearing structure: walls carry loads; economical up to 3–4 storeys. Framed structure: beams & columns carry loads; walls are only partitions/panels.
Loads: dead, live (imposed), wind, snow, earthquake, thermal. Typical live loads: residential floor 2 kN/m², office 2.5–4 kN/m², accessible roof 1.5 kN/m².
Occupancy groups (NBC): A residential, B educational, C institutional, D assembly, E business, F mercantile, G industrial, H storage, J hazardous.
Areas: plinth area = built-up covered area at floor level; carpet area = usable area excluding walls, stairs, lifts, verandahs, toilets; circulation area ≈ 10–20% of plinth area.

Fig. 1.1 — Components of a building: substructure, plinth, DPC, wall, lintel, chajja, roof slab, parapet, coping.

s.t: Unit weights of common materials (for dead load)
b: Plinth protection: ≈ 0.6–1.0 m wide sloping concrete apron around the building to keep rain water away from the foundation.
Plinth beam: RCC beam at plinth level tying columns/walls; resists differential settlement and acts as a seismic band.
Load-bearing vs framed: Load-bearing: thick walls at lower floors, less flexibility, cheaper for 1–3 storeys. Framed: thin walls, open plans, any height, better under earthquakes.
Building life: Permanent RCC/masonry buildings are usually designed for ≈ 50–100 years; temporary/semi-permanent for less.
💡 Exam point: Plinth level divides substructure (below) from superstructure (above). DPC is laid at plinth level.
Exploration methods: test pits (shallow, ≤ 3 m), auger boring, wash boring, percussion drilling, rotary drilling, probing; geophysical — seismic refraction, electrical resistivity.
SPT: 63.5 kg hammer, 75 cm free fall, split-spoon sampler; N = blows for last 30 cm of 45 cm penetration.
Plate load test: square steel plate 30–75 cm, 25 mm thick; gives bearing capacity and settlement. Not reliable for clays (short-term).
Safe bearing capacity: ultimate BC ÷ factor of safety (2–3).
Minimum depth of foundation: 50 cm (IS 1080); below zone of seasonal moisture change / frost.
Black cotton soil: expansive clay (montmorillonite); swells on wetting, shrinks on drying — use under-reamed piles.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Depth of exploration: At least 1.5 × width of the footing below foundation level (for raft ≈ 1.5–2 × width), or until hard stratum.
Area ratio of sampler: Ar = (Do² − Di²)/Di² × 100; ≤ 10–20% for undisturbed samples (thin-walled Shelby tube).
SPT corrections: Overburden correction and dilatancy correction for fine/silty sand below water table: N′ = 15 + ½(N − 15) when N > 15.
Static cone penetration (Dutch cone): 60° cone, 10 cm² base area, pushed at ≈ 2 cm/s; gives cone resistance qc — good for sands.
Vane shear test: In-situ undrained shear strength of soft, sensitive clays.
Terzaghi’s bearing capacity (strip): qu = cNc + γDfNq + 0.5γBNγ. Square: 1.3cNc + γDfNq + 0.4γBNγ. Circular: 1.3cNc + γDfNq + 0.3γBNγ.
Plate load test → footing settlement: Sand: Sf = Sp·[B(Bp + 0.3)/(Bp(B + 0.3))]². Clay: Sf = Sp·(B/Bp).
💡 Exam point: Plate load test is unreliable for clays (short duration, small plate); SPT is mainly for sands; vane shear for soft clays.
Spread / isolated footing: one column; stepped or sloped.
Combined footing: two or more columns. Rectangular — equal loads; Trapezoidal — larger load near property line.
Strap (cantilever) footing: two footings joined by a strap beam; used when exterior column is at property line.
Raft / mat: single slab under whole building; used when footings cover > 50% of plan area, low BC, or to reduce differential settlement.
Grillage: tiers of steel joists (or timber) embedded in concrete; heavy column loads on low-BC soil.
Inverted arch: arches inverted between piers; old practice, now rare.
Pile: when hard stratum is deep, soil is compressible, or uplift / lateral loads exist.
Piles by function: end-bearing, friction, compaction, tension (uplift), anchor, batter (inclined loads), fender (protect waterfront structures), sheet piles (retain soil / cut-off).
Piles by material: timber, concrete (precast; cast-in-situ — Raymond, Simplex, Franki, Vibro, Pedestal, MacArthur), steel (H, pipe, screw), composite.
Under-reamed pile: bulb dia = 2–2.5 × stem dia; spacing ≥ 2 × bulb dia; for black cotton soil.
Engineering News formula: Q = WH / [6(S + C)]; C = 2.5 cm (drop hammer), 0.25 cm (steam hammer); FoS = 6. Hiley’s formula — more accurate.
Negative skin friction: downward drag when soil around pile settles (fill over soft clay).

Well (caisson) foundation: bridges/heavy structures in rivers. Shapes — circular (most common), double-D, dumbbell, twin-circular, rectangular. Parts — cutting edge, curb, steining, bottom plug, sand filling, top plug, well cap.
Well tilt & shift limits: tilt 1 in 80 (IS 3955 / MoRTH specification; some books quote 1 in 60); shift ≤ 150 mm.
Timbering of trenches: stay bracing (firm soil), box sheeting (loose soil), vertical sheeting (deep, soft soil), runners (very loose), sheet piling (wet/soft).
Dewatering: sumps/ditches, well points (sand), deep wells, electro-osmosis (silts/fine soils), freezing, cement/chemical grouting.
Causes of foundation failure: unequal settlement, lateral escape of soil, shrinkage of soil, atmospheric action, withdrawal of moisture, tree roots.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 3.1 — Shallow foundations in plan: isolated, combined (rectangular & trapezoidal), strap and raft.
Fig. 3.2 — Under-reamed pile (for black cotton soil) and parts of a well (caisson) foundation.
Pile group efficiency (Converse–Labarre): η = 1 − θ[(n − 1)m + (m − 1)n] / (90 m n), where θ = tan⁻¹(d/s) in degrees; m = rows, n = piles per row.
Group capacity in clay: Lesser of (i) n × single-pile capacity × η and (ii) block failure capacity of the group.
Pile cap: Piles embedded ≈ 75–150 mm into cap; cap projects ≈ 100–150 mm beyond outer piles.
Pile load tests: Initial test (on test pile, to 2.5 × working load) and routine test (on working pile, to 1.5 × working load).
Driven vs bored piles: Driven: displacement, compacts loose sand, noisy. Bored (cast-in-situ): no vibration, suits built-up areas and clays.
Mat (raft) types: Flat plate, plate thickened under columns, beam-and-slab, cellular/box raft, piled raft.
Floating (compensated) foundation: Weight of soil excavated ≈ weight of building, so net pressure on soil is very small.
Well tilt correction: Eccentric grabbing, eccentric kentledge (loading), water/air jetting on higher side, pulling, strutting.
Grip length: Depth of well below maximum scour level; usually ≥ 1/3 of maximum scour depth.
💡 Exam point: Strap footing → exterior column at property line. Trapezoidal combined footing → heavier column near property line. Raft → footings cover > 50% of area.
Standard (modular) brick: 19 × 9 × 9 cm; nominal 20 × 10 × 10 cm. Pakistan standard: 9″ × 4½″ × 3″ (≈ 225 × 112.5 × 75 mm).
Bricks per m³: ≈ 500 modular bricks (with mortar). Weight of one brick ≈ 3–3.5 kg.
Frog: depression 10–20 mm on top face; forms key for mortar; laid upward.
Common terms: header (length ⟂ wall face), stretcher (length ∥ face), course, bed joint, perpend (vertical joint), lap, quoin (external corner), toothing, racking back.
Closers: queen closer (half width, cut lengthwise), king closer (one corner cut), bevelled closer, mitred closer.
Bats: half bat, three-quarter bat, bevelled bat.
Stretcher bond: all stretchers; for half-brick (11.5 cm) walls/partitions.
Header bond: all headers; for curved walls and footings.
English bond: alternate courses of headers and stretchers; queen closer after quoin header; strongest bond; no continuous vertical joint.
Flemish bond: header and stretcher alternately in each course; better appearance, slightly weaker than English. Double Flemish — both faces; Single Flemish — face Flemish, backing English.
English garden wall bond: one header course after 3–5 stretcher courses.
Raking bond: bricks laid at an angle in thick walls — diagonal bond and herring-bone bond.
Rat-trap (Silverlock’s) bond: bricks on edge with internal cavity; economical, insulating.
Soak bricks ≈ 2 h before use; frog upward; joints ≈ 10 mm; no continuous vertical joints.
Max height raised per day: ≈ 1.0–1.5 m; walls raised uniformly.
Efflorescence: white patches of soluble salts (from bricks/sand/water).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 4.1 — Brick bonds (elevations): stretcher, header, English and Flemish. Note the queen closer after the quoin header.
Fig. 4.2 — Closers (cut lengthwise) and bats (cut across). Queen closer = half width; king closer = one corner cut.
Brick manufacture (order): Unsoiling → digging → cleaning → weathering → blending → tempering → moulding → drying → burning.
Burning: Clamps (intermittent, poor quality) and kilns — intermittent kilns and continuous kilns (Bull’s trench, Hoffmann).
Good brick-earth: Alumina 20–30% (plasticity), silica 50–60% (prevents shrinkage/cracking), lime < 5%, iron oxide 5–6% (red colour), magnesia < 1%.
Harmful ingredients: Excess lime (melting, distortion), iron pyrites (crystallises, splits brick), alkalis (efflorescence), pebbles, organic matter.
Field tests of good brick: Clear ringing sound when two bricks are struck; no scratch by finger-nail; does not break when dropped flat from ≈ 1 m; uniform colour; sharp edges.
Wall thickness (Pakistan bricks): Half-brick ≈ 4½″ (≈ 11.5 cm), one-brick ≈ 9″ (≈ 23 cm), 1½-brick ≈ 13½″ (≈ 35 cm).
Bricks per m³ (Pakistan size): ≈ 390–400 bricks per m³ with 10 mm joints (before wastage). Modular bricks ≈ 500 per m³.
Special bricks: Fire bricks (refractory, alumina-silica), engineering bricks (dense, low absorption — DPC), perforated/hollow bricks (light, insulating), fly-ash bricks, sand-lime bricks.
💡 Exam point: English bond = strongest. Flemish bond = better appearance. Queen closer is placed next to the quoin header to break vertical joints.
Sanfoundry — 1000 Construction & Building Materials MCQs (chapter-wise) — bricks, stones, mortar, bonds
Rubble masonry: uncoursed (random), coursed, squared (coursed/uncoursed), polygonal, flint, dry rubble.
Ashlar masonry: finely dressed stones, joints ≤ 3 mm — ashlar fine, rough-tooled, rock/quarry-faced, chamfered, block-in-course.
Natural bed: stone laid with bedding planes perpendicular to load (horizontal in walls; radial in arches).
Through (bond) stones: run full wall thickness; ≈ one per 1.5–2 m² of wall face.
Composite masonry: two materials (e.g., brick-faced concrete, stone-faced brick).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Bridge piers, abutments, heavy engineering works, kerbs
Roofing, DPC, sills (splits into thin sheets)
Dressing of stone: Hammer-dressed, rough-tooled, chisel-dressed, punched-machine, rubbed, polished, quarry/rock-faced.
Quarrying methods: Hand tools/wedging, heating, and blasting (gunpowder for small, dynamite/gelignite for large).

Tests on stone: Crushing strength, water absorption, attrition (Deval), impact, hardness (Mohs), crystallisation, Smith’s test (soluble earthy matter), acid test (weathering of calcareous stones), Brard’s test (frost).
Specific gravity of building stones: ≈ 2.4–2.8 (most between 2.5 and 3.0).
Seasoning of stone: Newly quarried stone contains quarry sap; stored ≈ 6–12 months before use.
💡 Exam point: Natural bed: walls — horizontal; arches — radial (perpendicular to the line of thrust); cornices — vertical.
Cavity wall: two leaves with cavity 40–100 mm (usually 50–75 mm); ties ≈ 90 cm horizontally, 45 cm vertically, staggered. Advantages — damp prevention, heat & sound insulation.
Partition walls: brick (half-brick, reinforced), concrete, glass, timber, plaster slab, gypsum board, AC sheet, metal lath.
Retaining wall: holds soil; Breast wall: protects a cut slope from falling; Parapet: low wall on roof edge (≈ 1.0 m).
Coping: top course of wall shedding water; Corbel: projection supporting load; Cornice: horizontal moulded projection at roof level; String course: horizontal projecting course.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 6.1 — Cavity wall: two leaves, 50–75 mm cavity, staggered wall ties, DPC, weep holes.
Slenderness ratio (masonry): Effective height (or length) ÷ effective thickness; limited to about 27 for cement-mortar masonry (lower for lime mortar).
Retaining wall types: Gravity (masonry/plain concrete), cantilever (RCC, up to ≈ 6 m), counterfort (> ≈ 6 m), buttressed, crib, gabion.
Weep holes: Provided in retaining walls and breast walls to relieve water pressure; backed by a filter of graded material.
Partition wall requirements: Light, thin, strong enough for fixtures, sound-insulating, fire-resistant, and easy to erect/remove.
Veneered / faced walls: Facing bonded to backing (faced wall) vs facing only attached, not bonded (veneered wall).
💡 Exam point: Cavity width: 40–100 mm (usually 50–75 mm). Wall ties ≈ 90 cm horizontally, 45 cm vertically, staggered.
Arch terms: intrados (inner curve), extrados (outer curve), soffit, voussoirs (wedge units), keystone (crown), springing line, skewback, span, rise, haunch, spandrel, abutment, pier, impost.

By shape: flat, segmental (centre below springing), semi-circular (rise = ½ span), horse-shoe, pointed/Gothic (equilateral, lancet, drop), semi-elliptical (3- or 5-centred), stilted, Venetian, Florentine, Tudor, ogee, relieving.
Flat arch: skewbacks at 60° to horizontal (forms equilateral triangle); intrados given slight camber.
Relieving arch: built above flat arch / wooden lintel to relieve load.
By centres: one-, two-, three-, four-, five-centred.
Lintel: horizontal member over opening. Types — timber, stone, brick, RCC (most common), steel, reinforced brick.
Bearing of lintel: min 15 cm or depth of lintel, whichever is greater.
Chajja / sunshade: RCC projection over openings, ≈ 30–60 cm.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 7.1 — Arch terminology: intrados, extrados, voussoirs, keystone, springing line, skewback, haunch, spandrel, span and rise.
Modes of arch failure: Crushing of masonry, sliding of voussoirs, rotation (overturning) about an edge, and unequal settlement of abutments.
Load on lintel: Masonry above a lintel arches itself; only the triangular portion within 60° lines from the supports is taken as load on the lintel.
Centering: Temporary timber/steel framework supporting an arch until the mortar sets; struck (removed) gradually.
Arch materials: Rough brick arch (uncut bricks, wedge-shaped joints), gauged brick arch (cut bricks, thin joints), stone arch, concrete arch.
💡 Exam point: Flat arch: skewback at 60° to horizontal. Semicircular arch: rise = ½ span; centre lies on the springing line. Segmental arch: centre below the springing line.
Door size rules: width = 0.4–0.6 × height; height = width + 1.2 m. Common sizes — main door 1.0 × 2.0–2.1 m; internal 0.9 × 2.0 m; bath/WC 0.75 × 2.0 m.

Door types: battened & ledged; battened, ledged & braced; framed, ledged & braced; framed & panelled; glazed/sash; flush (solid, hollow, cellular core); louvred; wire-gauzed; revolving; sliding; swing; folding; pivoted; collapsible steel; rolling shutter.
Braces: inclined, lower end towards the hanging (hinge) side.
Door frame: horns (≈ 10–15 cm projections of head) fixed into wall; holdfasts — 3 per side.
Rolling shutters: shops, garages, godowns. Collapsible gates: security without blocking light.
Window area: ≥ 1/10 of floor area (bye-laws); ≈ 1/6 in hot-humid climates. Sill height ≈ 75–90 cm.

Window types: casement, double-hung sash (counterweights), pivoted, sliding, louvred, bay (projecting), corner, dormer (vertical window on sloping roof), gable, lantern (on flat roof), skylight (on sloping roof plane), clerestory (high on wall), fanlight (above door), ventilator.
Hardware: butt, T, strap, counterflap, H/pin and parliament hinges (door opens 180° clear of wall); tower bolt, aldrop, hasp & staple, mortice lock, latch, door closer, door stopper.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 8.1 — Door terminology (framed & panelled door): frame = head + horns + jambs; shutter = stiles + rails + muntin + panels.
Fig. 8.2 — Window terminology: head, horn, jamb, transom, mullion, sill, fanlight, glazing bars.
Fixed part built into the wall: head (top), jambs/posts (sides), sill/threshold (bottom).
Projection of the head beyond the jambs (≈ 10–15 cm), built into the wall for fixing.
Recess (≈ 12–15 mm) cut in the frame to receive the shutter.
Stile on the hinge side / stile on the lock side.
Rails from top to bottom; lock (middle) rail carries the lock; bottom rail is widest.
Vertical member between two rails dividing panels.
Vertical / horizontal member dividing a window (or door) frame.
Frame holding glass panes; sash bars (glazing bars) divide the glass.
Moulded strip covering the joint between frame and wall.
Mild-steel flat anchor fixing the frame into masonry — 3 per side.
Inclined slats (≈ 45°) allowing air but not rain or view.
Location of doors: Near room corners (≈ 20 cm away), minimum number, placed for good circulation and furniture arrangement; opposite openings help cross-ventilation.
Flush door cores: Solid core (block board / particle board), hollow core, cellular core (strips with voids).

Window glass types: Float/sheet, frosted (obscure), tinted, wired (fire, security), laminated (safety), toughened (≈ 4–5 × stronger, breaks into small blunt pieces), double glazing (heat & sound insulation).
Modern frames: Steel, aluminium, uPVC (no painting, good seal) besides timber.
💡 Exam point: Dormer window → sloping roof (vertical window). Skylight → in the sloping roof plane. Lantern → on a flat roof. Clerestory → high up in the wall. Fanlight → above a door/window transom.
Sanfoundry — MCQs on types of windows — casement, sliding, louvred, metal windows
Terms: tread (going), riser, nosing, flight, landing, winders, baluster, newel post, handrail, string/stringer, waist (slab thickness), headroom, pitch, scotia.

Types: straight, quarter-turn, half-turn (dog-legged — no well between flights; open-newel — well between flights), three-quarter turn, bifurcated, geometrical, circular/spiral (least space), helical.
Materials: RCC (most common, fire-resistant), stone, timber, steel, brick.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 9.1 — Stair terms: tread, riser, nosing, waist, pitch line, flight, landing, handrail, baluster, newel post, headroom.
Given: Floor-to-floor height 3.0 m, dog-legged stair, rise 150 mm, tread 250–300 mm.
Treads: Treads per flight = risers − 1 = 9; going of each flight = 9 × 300 = 2.7 m.

Requirements of a good stair: Well lit and ventilated; easy to reach (near entrance in public buildings); uniform risers & treads; no winders (if unavoidable, only at bottom); adequate width and headroom; handrails both sides if width > ≈ 1.5 m.
Lifts & escalators: Escalator incline ≈ 30° (max 35°), speed ≈ 0.5–0.75 m/s. Lifts needed for buildings over ≈ 4 storeys (bye-laws vary).
💡 Exam point: Winders are tapered steps used to change direction; avoid them. Spiral stair needs least space; dog-legged stair has no well between flights.
Ground floor components: compacted subgrade/fill, base course (lean concrete 1:4:8, ≈ 10 cm), floor finish.
Floor finishes: mud, brick, flagstone, cement concrete/IPS, terrazzo, mosaic, ceramic tiles, marble, granite, timber, rubber, linoleum, PVC/vinyl, asphalt, glass.
IPS (Indian Patent Stone): 25–50 mm cement concrete finish laid in panels (alternate bays).
Terrazzo: marble chips + cement (white/coloured) laid, ground and polished.
Linoleum: oxidised linseed oil + cork/wood flour on jute backing.

Upper floors: RCC slab (most common), flat slab, ribbed/waffle, hollow block, precast, jack-arch (brick arches on steel joists), timber floors — single joist (≤ 3.6 m), double joist (≤ 7.5 m), framed/triple (> 7.5 m).
Selection factors: cost, durability, damp-proofness, sound/heat insulation, hygiene, fire resistance, appearance, maintenance.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Granolithic, heavy-duty cement concrete, steel-chequered tiles
Granolithic flooring: Hard topping of cement + granite chips (1:1:2), laid on fresh concrete base — for heavy traffic.
Mosaic flooring: Small pieces of marble/tile set in cement; ground and polished.
Hollow-block / ribbed slabs: Lighter self-weight, better sound and heat insulation, economical for longer spans.
💡 Exam point: Cork flooring = noiseless (libraries, theatres). Granolithic = industrial heavy traffic. Terrazzo = hospitals & residences.
Roof terms: span, rise, pitch (rise/span), ridge, eaves, hip, valley, verge, gable, rafters (common, hip, valley, jack), purlin, cleat, batten, wall plate, ridge piece.
Special roofs: mansard (two slopes on each side), gambrel, hipped, gable, north-light / saw-tooth (factories — glazing faces north for uniform light), butterfly, shell, folded plate, dome.
Flat roof: RCC slab + terracing (lime concrete / mud phuska + tiles); drainage slope ≈ 1:40–1:100.
Roof coverings: thatch, tiles (Allahabad, Mangalore), slates, shingles, AC sheets, GI/CGI sheets, aluminium sheets.
GI/AC sheet laps: side lap 1–1½ corrugations; end lap ≈ 15 cm (min 7.5 cm on steep roofs).
Rainwater pipes: 75–150 mm dia; roughly one 100 mm pipe per ≈ 40 m² roof area.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 11.1 — Pitched roof terms in plan: ridge, hip, valley, eaves, verge, gable end.
Fig. 11.2 — King-post truss (≈ 5–8 m) and queen-post truss (≈ 8–12 m) with their members.
Steel truss types: Pratt, Howe, Fink (French), fan, Warren, north-light, bowstring, quadrangular, saw-tooth.
Pitch values: ¼ pitch ≈ 26.5°, ⅓ pitch ≈ 33.7°, ½ pitch = 45°. Tiled roofs need steeper pitch than sheet roofs.
Roof selection factors: Span, climate (rain/snow), materials available, fire resistance, insulation, appearance, cost.
Weathering course: Lime concrete/mud phuska layer laid to fall on flat roofs, topped by tiles — gives slope and insulation.
💡 Exam point: Hip = external angle where two slopes meet; Valley = internal angle; Verge = edge of roof at the gable; Eaves = lower edge of roof slope.
Causes of dampness: rising ground moisture (capillary), rain penetration, defective construction, condensation, leaking pipes.
DPC position: at plinth level, ≥ 15 cm above ground; horizontal DPC continuous over full wall width; vertical DPC in basements.
Flexible materials: hot bitumen, bituminous felt, mastic asphalt (semi-rigid), polythene, metal sheets (lead, copper).
Rigid materials: dense stone, engineering bricks, cement concrete (1:2:4 / 1:1.5:3, 25–40 mm thick) with waterproofing compound + 2 coats hot bitumen.
Methods: membrane DPC, integral (admixtures), surface treatment, cavity walls, guniting (cement-sand sprayed under pressure), pressure grouting, tanking (basements).
Anti-termite treatment: chemical soil treatment of trenches and plinth fill before construction.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Requirements of DPC material: Impervious, durable, flexible enough to resist cracking, strong enough for loads, not squeezed out, economical.
Mastic asphalt DPC: Laid hot in ≈ 20–25 mm thickness; impervious and durable; may squeeze out under heavy load in hot weather.
Bitumen felt DPC: Laid with ≈ 10 cm laps, on a levelled mortar bed; flexible but can be damaged during construction.
Anti-termite chemicals: Chlorpyrifos and similar emulsions in trench bottom, sides and plinth fill; older chemicals (aldrin, heptachlor, chlordane) are banned.
Tanking: Continuous waterproof membrane on basement floor & walls — external (preferred) or internal tanking.
💡 Exam point: DPC is placed at plinth level, ≥ 15 cm above ground; it must be continuous and should not be located at a joint in the floor.
Plaster thickness: external ≈ 20 mm (two coats), internal 12–15 mm, ceiling 6–10 mm; three-coat work 20–25 mm.

Special plasters: stucco (3 coats ≈ 25 mm, decorative), sand-faced, pebble-dash, rough-cast (spatter dash), plaster of Paris, gypsum, Keene’s cement (hard, polished — corners, skirting), barium plaster (X-ray rooms), acoustic plaster, Neeru finish (lime putty).
Plaster defects: blistering, cracking, efflorescence, flaking, peeling, popping, rust stains, softness, uneven surface.
Pointing: joints raked 10–20 mm deep and refilled with richer mortar (1:1–1:3). Types — flush, recessed, struck, weathered, V, beaded, keyed, rubbed, tuck (projecting band ≈ 3–5 mm).
Paint constituents: base (white lead, zinc oxide, red lead, titanium white), vehicle (linseed oil), drier, pigment, thinner (turpentine), extender/inert filler.
Types: oil, enamel, emulsion, plastic, distemper, cement paint, bituminous, aluminium, anti-corrosive; whitewash (lime), colour wash.
Varnish: oil, spirit (French polish = shellac in spirit), turpentine, water varnish.
Paint defects: blistering, chalking, cracking, crawling, flaking, grinning (background visible), saponification (alkali attack), wrinkling, bloom, fading, running, sagging.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 13.1 — Types of pointing (sections through the joint): flush, recessed, struck, weathered, V-groove, beaded, tuck.
Dry volume of mortar: Dry volume ≈ 1.27–1.33 × wet volume (bulkage of sand + voids).
Painting sequence (new woodwork): Surface preparation → knotting (shellac over knots) → priming → stopping (putty in holes) → undercoat → finishing coats.
Painting on new plaster: Allow plaster to dry and efflorescence to stop; use alkali-resistant primer, otherwise saponification occurs.
Distemper: Whiting (chalk) + glue/size + pigment; dry distemper (with water) and oil-bound (washable) types; cheaper than oil paint.
Covering capacity (approx.): Paints cover roughly 10–15 m² per litre per coat depending on surface.
💡 Exam point: Grinning = background visible through paint; Saponification = alkali attack forming soap; Blooming = dull patches; Flashing = glossy patches.
Materials: timber, plywood, steel, aluminium, plastic. Slip form — silos, chimneys, towers; jump/climbing form — high-rise cores.
Types: single (bricklayer’s / putlog), double (mason’s — stone work), cantilever/needle, suspended, trestle, steel tubular, patented.

Parts: standards (vertical, ≈ 2.5–3 m apart), ledgers (horizontal, ≈ 1.2–1.5 m vertical spacing), putlogs (≈ 1.2 m apart, one end in wall), transoms (both ends on ledgers), braces, boarding, guard rail, toe board.
Raking shores: inclined props (60°–75° to ground) supporting unsafe walls.
Flying shores: horizontal struts between two parallel walls (≈ up to 9 m apart) when one building is demolished.
Dead (vertical) shores: vertical props with needles through wall; for making openings / underpinning.
Purpose: strengthen/deepen existing foundation. Methods — pit method, pile method (jack piles, needle & pile), chemical consolidation (grouting).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 14.1 — Scaffolding parts: standards, ledgers, putlogs, boards, braces, guard rail.
Fig. 14.2 — Shoring: raking shore (leaning wall), flying shore (between two walls), dead shore (making openings).
Requirements of formwork: Strong for wet concrete + live load, rigid (no deflection), leak-proof joints, easy to remove without damage, re-usable, economical.
Loads on formwork: Weight of wet concrete (≈ 24–25 kN/m³), reinforcement, workers & equipment (live load), impact/vibration, lateral pressure of fresh concrete on vertical forms.
Release agents: Oil/emulsion applied to form face so it strips cleanly.
Underpinning — when needed: Foundation settled, building to be raised, adjacent deeper excavation, change of use with heavier loads.
💡 Exam point: Raking shore: rakers at 60°–75°. Flying shore: no ground support, between walls up to ≈ 9 m apart. Dead shore: vertical props + needles.

Principles of planning: aspect, prospect, privacy, grouping, roominess, furniture requirement, sanitation, flexibility, circulation (horizontal — corridors; vertical — stairs/lifts), elegance, economy, practical considerations.
Orientation (northern hemisphere, e.g. Pakistan): long walls facing north–south; minimise east–west exposure; living rooms south for winter sun; kitchen on east (morning sun).
FAR / FSI: total covered area of all floors ÷ plot area.
Plot coverage: ground-floor covered area ÷ plot area × 100.
Typical minimum sizes (NBC): habitable room 9.5 m², width 2.4 m, height 2.75 m; kitchen 5.0 m², width 1.8 m; bath 1.8 m²; WC 1.1 m²; bath/WC height 2.2 m.
Open spaces / setbacks: front, rear and side margins fixed by local authority (LDA, CDA, KDA etc.).
Building codes: Building Code of Pakistan (BCP) — seismic provisions BCP SP-2007, updated BCP-2021; NBC (India) and IBC often referenced.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
FAR example: Plot 500 m²; building of 3 floors × 250 m² = 750 m² → FAR = 750/500 = 1.5. Ground coverage = 250/500 = 50%.

Aspect / prospect / privacy: Aspect = arrangement of doors & windows to get sun, light, breeze; Prospect = view from windows (and impression from outside); Privacy = internal (between rooms) and external (from neighbours/street).
Grouping & circulation: Related rooms grouped together (kitchen–dining); circulation area should be short, straight, well lit; ≈ 20–25% of plinth area for corridors/stairs in public buildings.
Light & ventilation: Window area ≥ 1/10 of floor area (≈ 1/6 hot-humid); no part of room should be > ≈ 7.5 m from a window.

Pakistan codes: Building Code of Pakistan 2021 (based on IBC 2021), Building Code of Pakistan — Fire Safety Provisions 2016, Green Building Code of Pakistan 2023; local bye-laws by LDA, CDA, KDA, Peshawar Development Authority and TMAs.
💡 Exam point: FAR (FSI) = total covered area of all floors ÷ plot area. Ground coverage uses only the ground-floor covered area.

Fire-resisting materials: brick (best), concrete, asbestos, gypsum. Poor — timber (treat with Abel’s process: sodium silicate), steel (loses ≈ half strength at ≈ 550°C), glass (wired glass better), granite (cracks), limestone (disintegrates — calcines).
Fire load: calorific value of combustibles per unit floor area (kJ/m²); decides fire-resistance grading.
Fire-safety provisions: fire exits, external fire escape stairs, travel distance limits, fire doors, compartmentation, sprinklers, hydrants, wet/dry risers, smoke detectors, alarms.
Fire classes: A — ordinary combustibles (water); B — flammable liquids (foam, CO₂, dry powder); C — gases (dry powder) / electrical in US system (CO₂); D — metals (special dry powder).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Foam, CO₂, dry powder — NOT water jet
Dry powder; shut off gas supply
Fire-resistance rating: Time (hours) for which an element keeps stability, integrity and insulation in a standard fire test.
Fire-resistant construction: Adequate concrete cover to steel, encasing steel columns in concrete/gypsum, fire doors (self-closing), compartment walls, protected escape stairs.
Concrete in fire: Loses strength progressively above ≈ 300°C; at very high temperature (≈ 1000°C) strength falls to a small fraction of the original.
💡 Exam point: Brick is the best fire-resisting material; granite cracks and limestone calcines; steel loses ≈ half its strength around 550°C.
Sabine’s formula: T = 0.16 V / A (SI); A = Σαs (total absorption, in sabins). 1 open window sabin: α = 1.
Ideal reverberation time: speech 0.5–1.0 s; music 1.0–2.0 s.
Echo: reflected sound arriving > 1/15 s (≈ 0.067 s) after direct sound; path difference ≈ 23 m (343 m/s × 1/15 s); the classic '17 m' figure is the reflector distance for 1/10 s persistence.
Acoustic defects: echo, reverberation, sound foci, dead spots, insufficient loudness, external noise, resonance.
Absorbent materials: acoustic tiles, fibre boards, perforated boards, acoustic plaster, curtains, carpets, upholstered seats.
Audible range: 20 Hz – 20 kHz. Sound insulation by mass (heavy walls), cavity/double walls, floating floors, sealing gaps.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Inverse-square law: Sound level falls by ≈ 6 dB for every doubling of distance from a point source.
Noise Reduction Coefficient (NRC): Average absorption coefficient at 250, 500, 1000 and 2000 Hz.
Remedies for defects: Echo — absorbent rear wall; long reverberation — add absorbers; sound foci — avoid concave surfaces; dead spots — reflectors; external noise — insulation and sealing.
💡 Exam point: Sabine: T = 0.16 V/A (V in m³, A in m² sabins). Unit of absorption = sabin (1 m² of open window, α = 1).

Causes of cracks: moisture movement, thermal movement, elastic deformation, creep, chemical action (sulphate attack, steel corrosion, alkali-aggregate reaction), foundation settlement, vegetation (tree roots).
Expansion joints: buildings longer than ≈ 45 m (IS 456); joint width ≈ 25–40 mm.
Construction joint: where concreting stops; located at points of minimum shear.
Earthquake-resistant masonry: plinth, lintel, roof and gable bands; vertical steel at corners and junctions; openings ≥ 600 mm from corners; symmetric plan; avoid heavy roofs and overhangs.
Soft storey: storey with much lower stiffness (e.g., open ground-floor parking) — vulnerable.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Diagonal cracks near corners/openings; wider at top or bottom
Cracks at roof–wall junction, long walls; provide expansion joints
Fine map/hair cracks in plaster & concrete; proper curing
Cracks along bars, spalling cover; adequate cover & dense concrete
Expansion, cracking of brickwork mortar; use SRC/cement low in C₃A
Cracks near trees; keep trees away from foundations
Confined masonry: Masonry walls built first and then confined by RCC tie-columns and tie-beams — good seismic performance for low-rise buildings.
Short-column effect: Columns partially restrained by infill/mezzanine attract high shear and fail in brittle manner.
Strong column – weak beam: Plastic hinges should form in beams, not columns, to avoid storey collapse.
Pakistan seismic code: BCP 2007 Seismic Provisions (based on UBC-97) replaced by Building Code of Pakistan 2021 (based on IBC 2021).
💡 Exam point: Seismic bands in masonry: plinth band, lintel band (most important), roof band, gable band; vertical bars at corners and junctions.
Power shovel: digs above its own level (hard soil). Backhoe (hoe): digs below its level (trenches, basements).
Dragline: long reach, below its level, soft/wet soil. Clamshell: vertical, deep, confined excavation in loose material.
Bulldozer: push earth ≈ 30–90 m; Scraper: cut, haul, spread (≈ 150–1500 m); Motor grader: levelling, shaping; Ripper: loosens hard ground.
Rollers: smooth-wheel (granular, finishing), sheepsfoot (cohesive soils), pneumatic-tyred (most soils), vibratory (granular).
Cranes: tower (high-rise), crawler, truck/mobile, derrick, gantry. Hoists, forklifts, concrete pumps, transit mixers, batching plants.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Choice of compactor: Cohesive soil → sheepsfoot / padfoot; granular → vibratory smooth-drum; mixed → pneumatic-tyred; finishing of asphalt → smooth-wheel (tandem).
Excavator output (approx.): Output = bucket capacity × fill factor × cycles per hour × job efficiency.
Swell & shrinkage of earth: Loose (excavated) volume > bank volume > compacted volume; swell for common earth ≈ 25%.
Concrete equipment: Batching plant, transit mixer, concrete pump/boom placer, needle (internal) vibrators, screed (surface) vibrators, shutter (form) vibrators.
💡 Exam point: Power shovel digs above its track level; backhoe below; dragline – soft wet soils at a distance; clamshell – vertical confined digging (wells, cofferdams).
Strongest brick bond: English bond. Best appearance: Flemish bond.
Half-brick partition wall: stretcher bond. Curved walls: header bond.
Max risers per flight: 12 (min 3). Min headroom: 2.1 m.
King post up to ≈ 8 m; queen post up to ≈ 12 m.
Grillage foundation: heavy column loads on poor soil.
Raking shore angle: 60°–75°. Flying shore: between two walls.
Lintel bearing: ≥ 15 cm. DPC: at plinth level.
Barium plaster: X-ray rooms. Keene’s cement: hard, polished surfaces.
Echo time limit: 1/15 s. Sabine: T = 0.16 V/A.
Grillage foundation: Transfers heavy steel-column loads to soil of low bearing capacity.
Stairs in public buildings: Located near the entrance.
Least bearing capacity: Moist (soft) clay; highest: hard rock.
Opening in sloping roof parallel to roof surface: Skylight; vertical window projecting from sloping roof: dormer.
Supporting an existing structure from underneath: Underpinning; temporary support of an unsafe structure: shoring.
Header: Brick laid with its length perpendicular to the wall face; stretcher — length parallel.
Monumental buildings: Marble; bridge piers — granite; roofing — slate.

Traps: P-trap (outlet horizontal, wash basins/WCs on walls), Q-trap (outlet at ≈ 45°, upper floors), S-trap (outlet vertical, floor-connected WC), gully trap (kitchen/bath waste outside), intercepting trap (last manhole before public sewer), floor trap (nahani trap), bottle trap.
Water seal: Depth of water in a trap preventing foul gases: ≈ 25–75 mm (≈ 50 mm common for WCs).
Loss of seal: Siphonage (self & induced), evaporation, back-pressure, capillary action, wind effect, leakage.
Plumbing systems: Two-pipe (separate soil & waste pipes, each with vent), one-pipe (single stack, all traps vented), single-stack (no separate vent), partially vented single stack.
Anti-siphonage pipe: Vent connected near the trap crown to preserve the water seal.
Vent pipe: Carried ≈ 1–1.5 m above the roof (or above nearby windows), with a cowl.
Manholes: At every change of direction, gradient, junction and pipe size; on straight runs at intervals (≈ 30 m for small sewers, larger for big sewers).
House drain slopes: 100 mm drain ≈ 1 in 40 to 1 in 60; 150 mm ≈ 1 in 60 to 1 in 100 (self-cleansing velocity ≈ 0.6–0.75 m/s).
Septic tank: Detention ≈ 24 hours; length:width ≈ 2:1 to 4:1; effluent to soak pit / dispersion trench.
Overhead tank & pipes: GI, PPR, uPVC, HDPE pipes; overhead tank to hold ≈ one day’s demand (≈ 135 L/person/day for residences, a common design value).
💡 Exam point: Intercepting trap is provided in the last manhole of a house drain before it joins the public sewer.
Seasoning: Natural (air) seasoning — slow, cheap; artificial — kiln, chemical, electrical, boiling, water seasoning. Target moisture ≈ 10–12% for joinery.
Defects: Knots, shakes (heart, cup, star, radial), rind galls, twisted fibres, upsets, warping, honeycombing; fungal (dry rot, wet rot) and insect (termites, beetles) attack.
Preservation: Tar, creosote, ASCU (arsenic–copper–chromium), solignum paints, Ascu treatment; Abel’s process (sodium silicate) for fire-resistance.
Joints in carpentry: Lap, butt, mortise-and-tenon (doors), dovetail (drawers, strong in tension), scarf (lengthening a member), bridle, housing, tongue-and-groove (boards/flooring).
Wood-based products: Plywood (odd number of veneers, grains at 90°), block board, particle board/chipboard, fibre board (hardboard, MDF), veneers, laminated timber.
💡 Exam point: Plywood always has an ODD number of plies with grains of adjacent plies at right angles — this balances it and prevents warping.
Prefabrication: Members (slabs, beams, wall panels) cast in factory/yard and erected at site — speed, quality control, less formwork; joints are the weak point.
Tilt-up construction: Wall panels cast flat on the floor slab and tilted up into position by crane.
Slip-form & jump-form: Continuous vertical concreting (silos, chimneys, cores) / climbing forms for tall cores.
Shotcrete / guniting: Concrete or mortar sprayed by compressed air — tunnels, slopes, repairs, swimming pools.
Light-gauge steel & EPS panels: Fast, light construction systems used for low-rise and rehabilitation housing.
BIM: Building Information Modelling — 3D digital model with data for design, quantity take-off, clash detection and facility management.

Green building: Energy-efficient envelope (insulation, shading, orientation), rain-water harvesting, solar energy, low-VOC materials, recycled materials. Pakistan: Green Building Code of Pakistan 2023 (PEC, based on IgCC 2021); rating systems such as LEED.
💡 Exam point: Building Code of Pakistan 2021 is based on IBC 2021; BCP Seismic Provisions 2007 were based on UBC 1997.

Observed N = 40 in saturated fine sand: N′ = 15 + ½(40 − 15) = 27.5.
10 m³ of modular brickwork at 500 bricks/m³ + 5% wastage = 5,250 bricks.
100 m² of 12 mm plaster, 1:4: wet volume 1.2 m³ → dry ≈ 1.2 × 1.33 = 1.6 m³ → cement = 1.6/5 × 1440 = 461 kg ≈ 9.2 bags; sand = 1.6 × 4/5 = 1.28 m³.

Opening 1.2 m in a 230 mm brick wall (γ = 19 kN/m³), wall above is high: load = equilateral triangle of area (√3/4) × 1.2² = 0.62 m² → W = 0.62 × 0.23 × 19 = 2.72 kN; M = WL/6 = 0.54 kN·m (plus lintel self-weight wL²/8).

Floor height 3.0 m, riser 150 mm → 20 risers; dog-legged stair with two flights of 10 risers (9 treads each); with 250 mm tread the going per flight = 9 × 0.25 = 2.25 m; check 2R + T = 550 mm (slightly low — use T = 300 mm → 600 mm ✔).
Span 8 m, ¼ pitch → rise 2 m; rafter length = √(4² + 2²) = 4.47 m; roof angle = 26.57°.
Hall volume 1000 m³, total absorption 100 m² sabins: T = 0.16 × 1000/100 = 1.6 s (too long for speech; add absorbers to bring ≈ 1.0 s).
